---
title: "Quiz: describing a keypoint"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Why does the descriptor not need to be invariant to rotation and zoom by itself?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the keypoint already know?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The keypoint carries a frame $(x, y, \sigma, \theta)$ that moves with the image. The window is sampled in this frame (centred, size ∝ σ, turned by θ), so translation, zoom and rotation are removed before the descriptor is computed. The descriptor only has to tolerate what is left: lighting, small frame errors, deformation, noise.
:::

---

**Q2.** An image is made twice as bright and 30 grey levels are added. What happens to a gradient-histogram descriptor (normalised), and to a binary descriptor?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Gradients of $2I + 30$; the order of two intensities.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Neither changes. The gradients double (the offset disappears in the derivative), and normalising to length 1 removes the factor 2. In the binary descriptor every comparison $I(\mathbf p) < I(\mathbf q)$ keeps its result under any increasing map.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why a 4 × 4 grid of cells, and not one histogram for the whole window?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A disc and a ring can have the same histogram of directions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
One histogram forgets **where** the gradients are, so very different windows (a disc, a star, a ring) can look the same. The cells keep coarse positions (which quarter of the window) while still tolerating small shifts inside each cell: a compromise between distinctiveness and robustness.
:::

---

**Q4.** Two 256-bit descriptors differ in 6 bits. Two unrelated ones typically differ in how many? Is the pair a likely match?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each bit of two unrelated strings agrees with probability ½.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Unrelated: about 128 ± 8 bits. Six is 15 standard deviations below: almost certainly the same point (or a repeated pattern).
:::

---

**Q5.** Without orientation assignment, a 90° rotation of the image makes the descriptor useless. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the 8-bin histograms?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every gradient turns by 90°, so every cell histogram shifts by two bins, and the cells themselves move to other places in the grid. The vector is a different one. With θ, the window is read relative to the dominant direction, which turns with the image, and the descriptor is the same again.
:::

---

**Q6.** When would you choose a binary descriptor over a gradient histogram?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Size and speed against distinctiveness.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When speed and memory matter more than the last bit of accuracy: video, many images on a small device, real-time tracking. Gradient histograms are more distinctive and more robust to blur and viewpoint changes, which matters for accurate registration and 3D reconstruction.
:::

---

**Q7.** Light-microscopy and electron-microscopy images of the same section are to be aligned. Why do standard descriptors often fail?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Is a bright structure bright in both?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The two modalities show different contrast: a structure bright in one can be dark or invisible in the other, so gradients reverse or disappear, and the descriptors of the same point differ. Options: sign-free orientation histograms, a few manual landmarks, or intensity-based registration with mutual information.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that for unit vectors $\|\mathbf a - \mathbf b\|^2 = 2 - 2\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Expand the square.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\|\mathbf a - \mathbf b\|^2 = \mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a - 2\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b + \mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b = 1 - 2\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b + 1$. So the Euclidean distance and the dot product (the NCC of normalised patches) rank candidates in the same order.
:::
